edits.html:
Benign Acute Childhood Myositis

Bilateral calf pain and tenderness after influenza · is the calf tender, and are strength and reflexes normal?

Source vignette Pt — 12 yo M, 2 days of severe pain in both calves; a week earlier he had fever, dry cough, sore throat and headache that settled after 5 days of ibuprofen; now on no medication, afebrile (37 C), with marked tenderness of both calves · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned dermatomyositis, influenza-induced myositis, Kawasaki disease, parvovirus B19 arthritis and rheumatic fever
The decision point

Bilateral calf pain with marked calf tenderness, starting as a febrile respiratory illness resolves, is influenza-induced myositis. Influenza A or B can cause it, during the infection or after it. School-age boys are affected most. The child may walk on tiptoe or refuse to walk. Pain limits the gait, but strength and reflexes are normal. CK (creatine kinase) is elevated. A positive influenza test in this setting confirms the cause. Treatment is analgesia, fluids and rest, and recovery usually takes about a week.

Dark urine is the warning sign. A heme-positive dipstick with few red cells means myoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis. Admit for intravenous fluids and check creatinine and potassium.

Muscle or joint pain after a febrile illness in a child — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptKey discriminatorWhy less likely here
Influenza-induced myositis (benign acute childhood myositis)School-age child; calf pain during or just after influenza A or BBilateral calf tenderness, pain-limited gait, normal strength and reflexes, elevated creatine kinaseFits: tender calves a week after a flu-like illness
Growing painsAges 3 to 12; recurrent evening or night leg pain with pain-free daysNormal examination, no tendernessAcute onset after an illness, and the calves are tender
Guillain-Barré syndrome Can't missAscending paralysis after an infectionTrue weakness with absent reflexesPain and muscle tenderness, with no weakness described
DermatomyositisInflammatory myopathy with skin findingsProximal weakness, heliotrope rash, Gottron papulesNo rash; the pain is in the calves, not proximal weakness
Kawasaki diseaseVasculitis of young childrenFever for 5 days or more plus conjunctivitis, rash, lymphadenopathy, extremity and lip changesAfebrile now, with none of the mucocutaneous findings
Parvovirus B19 arthritisArthritis or arthralgia with or without the slapped-cheek rashSymmetric small joints of the hands, wrists and feetThe pain and tenderness are in muscle, not joints
Acute rheumatic feverFollows untreated group A streptococcal pharyngitisCarditis, arthritis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, choreaNone of these findings; calf muscle tenderness is not a criterion
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Calf and neurologic examinationFirstCalf tenderness, normal strength and reflexesMyositis; a normal examination fits growing pains; weakness with absent reflexes suggests Guillain-Barré syndrome
Serum creatine kinaseConfirmsElevatedMuscle injury, placing the problem in muscle rather than joint or nerve
Influenza testCausePositive for influenza A or BInfluenza-induced myositis, with compatible symptoms and an elevated creatine kinase
Urinalysis with microscopyNextHeme-positive dipstick with few red cellsMyoglobinuria from rhabdomyolysis: intravenous fluids, creatinine and potassium
Electromyography, muscle MRI or biopsySkipNot needed in a typical caseTender calves, elevated creatine kinase and a recent flu-like illness make the diagnosis
Scenario bank
Pearls How NBME framed it: the stem never names influenza, and the key names the cause, influenza-induced, rather than the syndrome · Calf tenderness on palpation is incompatible with growing pains, which require a normal examination · Guillain-Barré syndrome causes true weakness with lost reflexes; this myositis leaves strength and reflexes intact · Avoid aspirin in a child with influenza because of the risk of Reye syndrome
Pairs with Part I Benign Limb Pain in a Child also presents as bilateral calf pain in a school-age child, but the examination is normal. Part I Hemoglobinuria: the Dipstick-Microscopy Mismatch owns the heme-positive dipstick with few red cells that marks rhabdomyolysis. Store the discriminator as a question: is the calf tender?
Transferable rule In a child with bilateral calf pain, examine the calves. Tenderness after a febrile respiratory illness points to viral myositis. A normal examination points to growing pains.
Class-vs-memberDermatomyositis is also a myositis, but it causes proximal weakness with a heliotrope rash and Gottron papules.
Salient decoyKawasaki disease needs 5 or more days of fever plus mucocutaneous findings; this child had fever without those findings, and it has resolved.
Unchecked attributeParvovirus B19 arthritis affects the small joints of the hands, wrists and feet; this pain is in the calf muscles.
True-fact-wrong-slotRheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis and causes carditis, arthritis, nodules, erythema marginatum or chorea, not calf myositis.
